title: Aldersgate (1738)
hook: at a quarter to nine, Wesley feels his heart strangely warmed

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Wesley in the storm, watching families sing as the waves broke. Your line was they were not afraid.

"In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." That's John Wesley, back in London after Georgia. The mission didn't go well. He's come home discouraged, still haunted by the calm he saw on that ship, still asking what those Moravian families knew. A society, in his world, is a small group meeting in a room to pray and read. He doesn't want to go. He goes anyway. Someone is reading aloud from an old book: Martin Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. Not a thrilling evening, on paper.

A little further on, in his own words: "About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed." He goes on: he felt he did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation, and an assurance was given him that his sins were taken away, even his. Three things stand out. First, the time. Wesley, the man of schedules, notes it, about a quarter before nine, the way you'd remember where you were when the phone rang with news. Second, strangely. Not dramatic or loud: strange, unfamiliar, perhaps something he hadn't felt that way before, from a man who'd been doing religious things all his life. Third, warmed. Not blazing. Warmed. In Luke's gospel, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who explains the scriptures to them. Only later do they realize it was the risen Jesus, and they say to each other, "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" Wesley's evening has the same shape: words read aloud, and a heart that responds before the head has caught up. Methodists remember this evening, and Christians in other churches tell the story too. But hear what came before and after. Before, a man who had tried hard, gone unwillingly, and been honest about his fear. After, as his journal shows, he still had doubts and dry days. Aldersgate wasn't the end of the road. It was a turn in it.

Look back over the last week for a moment, maybe a small one, when something in you warmed: a sentence someone said, a song, a kindness, a line you read. Don't judge it as big or small; just find it and stay with it, where you were, roughly what time. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, let yourself remember it fully.
Aldersgate. The street in London where, at a meeting he went to unwillingly, John Wesley felt his heart strangely warmed.
Your line: a quarter before nine. Not blazing, just strangely warmed. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some Methodist and Wesleyan churches mark Aldersgate Day by reading Wesley's journal entry aloud, and some Christians keep a habit of reviewing the day each evening to notice where God met them.

Editor: fixed the garbled closing line ('the moment his heart turned toward it', with no clear referent) to 'a turn in it'; softened the claim that the warmth was something he had never felt before.

Second editor pass: cut 'the sentence that made this room famous' (a fact about the text's fame the journal doesn't state); myth item 'almost to the minute' became 'to the quarter hour', since he wrote 'about a quarter before nine'.
Audit: 'notes the exact quarter hour' contradicted his own 'about a quarter before nine'; now says the time as he wrote it.
